# Opioid use disorder

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Toxic and metabolic disorders > Opioid use disorder*

[Original Article Link](/library/bt0HX3)

---

## Summary

<u>Opioid use disorder</u> (<u>OUD</u>) is a chronic disease characterized by physical and psychological dependence on prescription and/or nonprescription <u>opioids</u>. The <u>prevalence</u> of <u>OUD</u> in the United States has risen sharply in recent decades. Core clinical features of <u>OUD</u> are a persistent pattern of maladaptive behaviors related to the pursuit and use of <u>opioids</u>, including use despite adverse consequences and a preoccupation with obtaining <u>opioids</u>. Diagnosis is based on <u>DSM-5</u> criteria. <u>Medication-assisted treatment</u> is the cornerstone of management, combining <u>medications for opioid use disorder</u> with individualized psychosocial treatment. Long-acting <u>opioid</u> <u>agonists</u> (i.e., <u>methadone</u> or <u>buprenorphine</u>) are most commonly used and have comparable long-term outcomes for addressing cravings and <u>opioid withdrawal syndrome</u> (<u>OWS</u>) and reducing the risk of overdose. <u>Naltrexone</u> may be appropriate for patients trying to abstain from <u>opioid</u> use. <u>OUD</u> is a highly stigmatized lifelong condition that requires a strong <u>therapeutic alliance</u> and <u>patient-centered approach</u> to address relapses, comorbid conditions (e.g., <u>PTSD</u>, infectious complications of injecting drugs), and other circumstances that may impact <u>treatment adherence</u>.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Risk factors</u> for prescription <u>opioid</u> misuse include: [[3]](/library/9s1NCR0)

* History of prior or current <u>substance use disorder</u> (strongest predictor)

* <u>Family history</u> of <u>SUD</u>

* History of prior or current psychiatric disorders/mental health disorders (e.g., <u>anxiety</u>, <u>depression</u>)

* Severe <u>pain</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

<u>Opioid</u> <u>agonists</u> bind at κ-, δ-, and <u>μ-opioid receptors</u> throughout the body. Clinical features of <u>OUD</u> (e.g., physical dependence and compulsive use) result from repeated stimulation of <u>μ-opioid receptors</u> in the <u>brain</u>.




### Acute use [[4]](/library/kscmEd0)[[5]](/library/OscIEd0)




* <u>Opioids</u> bind to <u>μ-opioid receptors</u> in the <u>locus coeruleus</u> → inhibition of <u>cAMP</u> → ↓ <u>norepinephrine</u> release

* ↑ <u>Dopamine</u> in <u>mesolimbic</u> reward circuits → euphoria





### Long-term use [[4]](/library/kscmEd0)[[5]](/library/OscIEd0)




Long-term <u>opioid</u> use leads to upregulation of the <u>cAMP</u> pathway (to offset inhibition resulting from <u>opioids</u>), resulting in:




* Tolerance

* Ongoing stimulation of <u>μ-opioid receptors</u> is required to maintain normal levels of <u>norepinephrine</u>.

* Increasingly higher <u>opioid</u> doses are needed to achieve <u>analgesic</u>, euphoric, and sedative effects.

* Dependence: absent or diminished stimulation of <u>μ-opioid receptors</u> → ↑ <u>norepinephrine</u> levels → <u>OWS</u>





### <u>Opioid</u> cessation [[4]](/library/kscmEd0)




* Hyperactivity in the <u>locus coeruleus</u> → excessive release of <u>norepinephrine</u> → <u>OWS</u>

* See “Pathophysiology” in “<u>Opioid withdrawal</u>” for details.

---

## Clinical features

* Tolerance, dependence, craving, compulsive use

* Social impairment (e.g., unable to fulfill family, work, or school obligations)

* <u>Opioid</u>-induced disorders, e.g.:

* <u>Depressive disorder</u>, <u>anxiety disorder</u>

* <u>Sleep disorders</u>

* <u>Sexual dysfunction</u>

* <u>Delirium</u>

* Opioid-induced neurotoxicity

* Acute <u>delirium</u>, <u>myoclonus</u>, <u>hallucinations</u>, and/or <u>hyperalgesia</u>

* Thought to result from the accumulation of active metabolites of <u>morphine</u>, <u>hydromorphone</u>, or <u>hydrocodone</u>

---

## Management

### Approach [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)




* Identify and treat <u>opioid withdrawal syndrome</u>.

* Perform a comprehensive <u>SUD assessment</u>.

* Identify and treat concurrent substance use and psychiatric disorders.

* Offer or refer for <u>medication-assisted treatment</u>, i.e.:

* <u>Medication for opioid use disorder</u>   [[11]](/library/KidUsp0)

* Psychosocial treatment (e.g., <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u>)

* Consider referral for inpatient or residential management for high-risk patients.

* Initiate strategies for <u>harm reduction in OUD</u> and discuss relapse prevention.





> [!TIP]
> Use <u>person-centered language</u> to reduce stigma and engage patients. [[12]](/library/4013T20)




> [!WARNING]
> Do not withhold <u>medication for opioid use disorder</u> from patients who decline a psychosocial evaluation or if comprehensive addiction treatment is unavailable. [[13]](/library/Xsc9td0)




### Medication for OUD (<u>MOUD</u>) [[6]](/library/l01vT20)




<u>MOUD</u> involves the <u>treatment of OUD</u> with a long-acting <u>opioid</u> <u>agonist</u> (i.e., <u>methadone</u> or <u>buprenorphine</u>) or <u>antagonist</u> (i.e., <u>naltrexone</u>).  See “<u>Management of opioid withdrawal</u>” for details on initiating treatment for <u>OWS</u>.




* Higher success rates than abstinence-based treatment

* Initiate under medical supervision

* Continue for as long as the patient benefits from treatment.





> [!TIP]
> <u>OUD</u> is a chronic disorder. Treatment aims to prevent relapse of <u>unhealthy drug use</u>. [[6]](/library/l01vT20)




#### <u>Opioid</u> <u>agonist</u> therapy




* Induction phase

* Induction regimens vary but are generally similar to those used to treat <u>OWS</u>.

* See “<u>Methadone induction</u>” and “<u>Buprenorphine induction</u>” in “<u>Opioid withdrawal</u>” for dosages.

* <u>Maintenance therapy</u>

* May require higher doses than the induction phase [[6]](/library/l01vT20)

* <u>Methadone</u>: typically administered at a <u>methadone</u> clinic

* <u>Buprenorphine</u>: can be prescribed by any practitioner with a current DEA registration





> [!TIP]
> <u>Methadone</u> and <u>buprenorphine</u> have comparable long-term <u>efficacy</u> and safety outcomes. [[6]](/library/l01vT20)




#### <u>Opioid</u> <u>antagonist</u> therapy




* Indication: <u>maintenance therapy</u> for patients who have completed <u>opioid withdrawal</u> and want to abstain from <u>opioid</u> use

* Treatment options

* Oral <u>naltrexone</u> DOSAGE

* IM <u>naltrexone</u> DOSAGE administered by a <u>health care professional</u>





> [!WARNING]
> To avoid <u>precipitated withdrawal</u>, ensure <u>opioid</u> abstinence for 7–14 days prior to starting <u>naltrexone</u>. [[13]](/library/Xsc9td0)




### Harm reduction in OUD [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)[[14]](/library/TGc6Ad0)




* Educate patients on <u>opioid overdose prevention</u>, including:

* Safe use strategies, e.g.:

* Using <u>opioids</u> in the company of others and/or at a <u>supervised injection facility</u> [[15]](/library/lkdvLJ0)

* Safe <u>opioid</u> storage

* Use of <u>fentanyl testing strips</u> (if available)  [[16]](/library/USWb_k0)[[17]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Naloxone</u> prescription DOSAGE for <u>opioid overdose</u> reversal

* To reduce the risk of infections:

* Offer <u>hepatitis A vaccine</u> and <u>hepatitis B vaccine</u>.

* <u>Counsel on STI prevention</u>.

* For individuals who inject drugs:

* Educate on <u>safe injection practices</u>.

* Provide safe injection supplies and/or refer to a <u>syringe services program</u>.

* Offer <u>HIV PrEP</u> to patients with <u>HIV PrEP indications</u>.

* <u>Counsel on contraception</u> and offer <u>long-acting reversible contraception</u> to prevent <u>unintended pregnancies</u>.   [[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)





> [!TIP]
> Provide take-home <u>naloxone</u> kits to all patients with <u>OUD</u> and/or <u>risk factors for opioid overdose</u>. Train patients and close contacts in the use of <u>naloxone</u> for treating <u>opioid overdose</u>. [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)




### Relapse prevention [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)




* Identify and treat <u>OWS</u> symptoms.

* Follow up with patients regularly.

* Encourage patients to engage with <u>psychosocial counseling</u>.

* Optimize management of comorbid physical, psychiatric, and <u>substance use disorders</u>.

* Assist patients in identifying triggers for <u>opioid</u> use.

* Use <u>maintenance therapy</u> for <u>OUD</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Opioid withdrawal management</u> is not recommended without <u>maintenance therapy</u> for <u>OUD</u> because of the high risk of relapse. [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)

---

## Complications

* <u>Opioid withdrawal syndrome</u>

* <u>Opioid overdose</u>

* Infections in people who inject drugs (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>hepatitis C</u>, <u>endocarditis</u>, <u>skin and soft tissue infections</u>)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prevention

* Carefully weigh the <u>risks and benefits of opioid therapy</u> and avoid unnecessary prescription of <u>opioids</u>. For details, see:

* <u>Choice of analgesic for acute pain</u>

* <u>Management of chronic noncancer pain</u>

* When prescribing <u>opioids</u>, follow principles of <u>risk mitigation for opioid therapy</u>. For details, see:

* <u>Opioids for acute pain</u>

* <u>Opioids for chronic noncancer pain</u>

* Include <u>screening for SUD</u> as part of routine health care.

---

## Special patient groups

### OUD in pregnancy




#### Screening and diagnostics [[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)[[20]](/library/gQdFvp0)




* Verbally screen all pregnant individuals for <u>SUD</u> during the first prenatal visit.

* <u>Prenatal psychosocial screening</u> options include:

* <u>NIDA quick screen</u>

* <u>CRAFFT</u>

* <u>4Ps Plus</u>

* Screening <u>drug tests</u> are generally not recommended; obtain <u>informed consent</u> before testing for any drug use in <u>pregnancy</u>.  [[9]](/library/m01Vg20)[[21]](/library/3RdS5p0)

* <u>Diagnostics for OUD</u> are the same as in nonpregnant individuals.





> [!WARNING]
> State laws may mandate reporting of <u>substance use during pregnancy</u>. [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)




#### Management [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)[[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)[[20]](/library/gQdFvp0)[[22]](/library/1id2qp0)




The following modifications to the general <u>management of OUD</u> are recommended.




##### Prenatal management [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)[[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)[[22]](/library/1id2qp0)




Involve a multidisciplinary team to ensure the best outcomes for the patient and fetus.




* Educate patients about <u>complications of untreated OUD in pregnancy</u>.

* As part of <u>harm reduction in OUD</u>, encourage:

* Use of <u>naloxone</u> in the event of overdose

* <u>Smoking cessation</u>  [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)

* Refer for treatment with an addiction specialist.

* First-line: pharmacotherapy with <u>opioid</u> <u>agonists</u> (i.e., <u>methadone</u> and <u>buprenorphine</u>)

* The safety of other <u>opioid</u> treatment options (e.g., medically supervised <u>opioid withdrawal management</u>, <u>naltrexone</u>) is unclear in <u>pregnancy</u>.

* Consider hospitalization for the initiation of <u>MOUD</u> to reduce the risk of <u>adverse events</u>. [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)

* Provide additional tailored <u>prenatal care</u> as indicated, e.g.:

* <u>Third-trimester screening for STIs</u>

* Additional <u>prenatal ultrasounds</u> to assess for <u>intrauterine growth retardation</u>





> [!TIP]
> Although <u>opioid</u> <u>agonists</u> can cause <u>neonatal abstinence syndrome</u>, they are the preferred treatment option in <u>pregnancy</u> because they have a lower risk of adverse maternal and fetal outcomes than untreated <u>OUD</u>. [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)[[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)




##### Peripartum management [[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)[[22]](/library/1id2qp0)




* Continue <u>maintenance dose</u> of <u>opioid</u> <u>agonists</u> throughout <u>labor</u>.

* Offer <u>obstetric analgesia</u> to all individuals.

* Utilize multimodal <u>pain</u> relief, including regional <u>analgesia</u>, <u>NSAIDs</u>, and <u>acetaminophen</u>.

* If <u>opioids</u> are used:

* Higher doses are typically required because of <u>opioid</u> dependence.

* Avoid <u>butorphanol</u>, <u>nalbuphine</u>, or <u>pentazocine</u> because of the risk of precipitating withdrawal.

* Monitor <u>newborns</u> closely after <u>birth</u> for signs of <u>neonatal abstinence syndrome</u>.





##### Postpartum management [[7]](/library/sRdtop0)[[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)[[23]](/library/kEWmDM0)




* Ensure patients are connected to appropriate support services, including relapse prevention.

* Educate patients on safe <u>breastfeeding</u>.

* Patients can breastfeed if they: [[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)

* Are stable on <u>opioid</u> <u>agonists</u>

* Have no <u>contraindications to breastfeeding</u> (e.g., active blood-borne infections)

* Are not currently using <u>recreational drugs</u> or misusing prescription drugs

* Advise patients to stop <u>breastfeeding</u> if they relapse.





#### Complications of untreated OUD in pregnancy [[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)




* Disruptions to <u>prenatal care</u>

* <u>Intrauterine growth restriction</u>

* <u>Placental abruption</u>

* <u>Preterm labor</u>

* Intrauterine <u>meconium</u> passage

* Fetal <u>death</u>

* Low <u>infant</u> <u>birth</u> weight [[22]](/library/1id2qp0)

* <u>Neonatal abstinence syndrome</u>  [[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)





#### Prevention [[18]](/library/kRdmMp0)




* Offer <u>contraceptive</u> counseling and initiation of <u>long-acting reversible contraception</u> for patients with <u>OUD</u>.

* Avoid prescribing <u>opioids</u> in <u>pregnancy</u> whenever possible.

* If <u>opioids</u> are required, e.g., for acute severe <u>pain</u>, discuss risks and benefits for the pregnant individual and fetus.

* For patients with <u>chronic pain</u>, refer to a <u>pain</u> specialist if there is concern for developing <u>opioid tolerance</u>. [[21]](/library/3RdS5p0)
